record.title: Paper reports that language-model agents can organize context-learning loops from self-generated gameplay
record.summary: A November 17 preprint studies frozen language-model agents given a general goal to improve gameplay, basic tools for generating and testing games, and permission to edit text context. The authors report that newer models in three model families improve held-out gameplay without a prescribed optimization loop, and that one model's learned context transfers to different game settings and between model families. The experiments use small, controlled game benchmarks and report three teacher seeds per model; the paper does not establish open-ended or real-world recursive self-improvement, weight updates, or causal contribution of the observed learning strategies.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors submitted arXiv:2611.23219v1 on 17 November 2026, reporting a study of self-organized context optimization through self-generated gameplay.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the canonical PuzzleScript-t20 setting, the authors report held-out performance gains of 20% for Claude Opus-5, 10% for GPT 6-Astra, and 6% for GLM 5.3 over default-context players; the six-model comparison uses three teacher sessions per model, 20 text-context updates, and up to 150 gameplay calls.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For Claude Opus-5, the authors report that learned context transfers to PuzzleScript-t30 (+9%), ARC-AGI-L1 (+21%), and MazeBench path-efficiency score (+0.15); in three-seed PuzzleScript-t20 tests, artifacts transferred between Opus 5 and GPT 6-Astra.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that more effective self-improvers more often used direct A/B comparisons, generated fewer trivial games, and concentrated replays on games with intermediate observed win rates; an LLM judge scored alignment to a self-regulated-learning rubric, and the paper says this association does not establish a causal mechanism.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected paper does not establish self-improvement on open-ended real-world tasks, recursive weight updates, sustained improvement over much longer horizons, or safety behavior outside its controlled game setting.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent matched reproduction of the teacher-player experiments or reported performance changes was inspected.
The paper does not establish whether self-organized context learning transfers to open-ended scientific, coding, or other real-world work, nor whether it supports long-horizon recursive improvement.
Behavioral self-regulation scores and task-selection patterns correlate with improvement, but causal contribution is not identified; the paper also contains incomplete bibliography placeholders.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported behavior holds within the stated controlled-game regime, it materially changes agent-learning and post-training design by showing that a model can organize parts of its own context-learning procedure from self-generated experience; current results do not establish open-ended or real-world self-improvement.
limitations: Reported outcomes are author claims and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
The main setting is short-horizon puzzle gameplay; the authors state that extension to more open-ended domains with weaker model priors remains unknown.
Each model's canonical teacher result averages three independent sessions; transfer tests use small benchmark subsets and limited rollouts.
The paper reports correlations between learning-strategy annotations and performance but does not establish that those strategies cause improvement; one behavioral rubric is scored by GPT 6-Astra.
The arXiv HTML bibliography contains unresolved citation placeholders; no public code or data artifact was established in this activation.
brief.summary: A November 17 preprint studies frozen language-model agents given a general goal to improve gameplay, basic tools for generating and testing games, and permission to edit text context. The authors report that newer models in three model families improve held-out gameplay without a prescribed optimization loop, and that one model's learned context transfers to different game settings and between model families. The experiments use small, controlled game benchmarks and report three teacher seeds per model; the paper does not establish open-ended or real-world recursive self-improvement, weight updates, or causal contribution of the observed learning strategies.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report +20%/+10%/+6% held-out PuzzleScript-t20 improvement for Opus-5/GPT 6-Astra/GLM 5.3; for Opus-5, +9% PuzzleScript-t30, +21% ARC-AGI-L1, and +0.15 MazeBench SPL; learned context also transfers in both directions between Opus 5 and GPT 6-Astra.
technical.compute_or_cost: The reported teacher budget is 20 context updates and 150 gameplay calls per session; no real-world training-cost, deployment-economics, or sustained-compute result is established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible arXiv v1 paper specifies the experimental procedures, model matrix, budgets, evaluation-set sizes, reported results, and limitations. This activation did not independently reproduce the experiments.
technical.mechanism: A frozen teacher model receives a broad gameplay-improvement goal, limited edit and gameplay budgets, and tools to generate games and modify text artifacts supplied as context to a player instance of the same model. It organizes its own task generation, evaluation, and updates instead of following an externally prescribed optimization loop.
technical.novelty: Studies a frozen model organizing its own context-optimization procedure and generating its own training experience without a prescribed update loop, then tests transfer across game engines and between model families.
technical.regime: Paper experiments use Claude Opus-{4.6, 5}, GPT {5.6-Sol, 6-Astra}, and GLM-{4.7, 5.3}; teacher and player use low reasoning effort and 20k tokens per response. The canonical PuzzleScript setting uses three teacher sessions per model, 20 context updates, 150 gameplay calls, a 20-turn horizon, and a 25k full-game token budget. Transfer evaluations include PuzzleScript-t30, ARC-AGI-3 Level 1, and 16 sampled MazeBench rooms.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares learned context with a default player context; its motivating GEPA comparison is author-reported and uses a prescribed loop on real in-distribution games under matched gameplay budgets, rather than an independent external reproduction.

brief.title: Paper reports that language-model agents can organize context-learning loops from self-generated gameplay
brief.why_it_matters: This is evidence about how much of an agent's learning procedure can be left to the agent itself: within a bounded game setting, the paper reports that agents can generate experience, test text changes, and improve held-out performance without a prescribed loop. It sharpens the self-improvement frontier while leaving transfer beyond games, long-run scaling, and safety implications unresolved.
